questions.q: A student finds a dark-coloured, heavy rock with visible interlocking crystals of pyroxene and plagioclase feldspar (each 3–5 mm) in a road cut in the Deccan Traps. Name the rock and state whether it is intrusive or extrusive.
questions.a: The rock is gabbro — intrusive, coarse-grained (phaneritic), mafic. A wrong answer of "basalt" reveals the student confuses composition with texture: basalt has the same minerals but is fine-grained (aphyric) because it cooled rapidly on the surface. If they say "extrusive", they have not linked crystal size to slow cooling at depth.

questions.q: Two rocks have identical mineral composition (50% plagioclase, 40% pyroxene, 10% olivine). Rock A has 1 mm crystals; Rock B has 5 mm crystals. Explain the geological history that produced this difference.
questions.a: Both rocks crystallised from the same mafic magma. Rock A cooled rapidly (likely as a lava flow or shallow dyke), giving insufficient time for crystal growth → aphanitic basalt. Rock B cooled slowly at depth (in a magma chamber or thick sill), allowing sustained diffusion and large crystals → phaneritic gabbro. A wrong answer citing "different magma" shows misunderstanding that texture reflects cooling rate, not composition.

questions.q: A hand specimen shows large, euhedral feldspar phenocrysts (1 cm) set in a fine-grained groundmass. The rock is light-coloured and contains quartz. Classify the texture and name the rock.
questions.a: Texture: porphyritic (bimodal grain size). Rock: granite porphyry (or rhyolite porphyry if groundmass is aphanitic and extrusive; but quartz + coarse phenocrysts suggest intrusive origin). Steps: 1) Note two distinct grain sizes → porphyritic. 2) Identify quartz + alkali feldspar → felsic. 3) Phenocrysts imply two-stage cooling: slow then fast. Wrongly calling it "gabbro porphyry" ignores the light colour and quartz, indicating mafic vs. felsic confusion.

questions.q: Compare the vesicular texture of a basalt from the Deccan Traps with the amygdaloidal texture of the same flow after hydrothermal alteration. What does each tell you about the magma and later history?
questions.a: Vesicles form when dissolved volatiles (H₂O, CO₂) exsolve as pressure drops during eruption; they indicate the magma was volatile-rich and erupted quickly. Amygdules form when those vesicles are later filled by secondary minerals (calcite, zeolites, quartz) from circulating hydrothermal fluids — evidence of post-emplacement fluid flow. A student who says "amygdules are primary gas bubbles" misses the secondary mineralisation step.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "All coarse-grained igneous rocks are granites." Use mineralogical and textural evidence to justify your answer.
questions.a: False. Coarse-grained (phaneritic) texture only indicates slow cooling. Composition determines the rock name: felsic phaneritic = granite; mafic phaneritic = gabbro; ultramafic phaneritic = peridotite. A student agreeing with the statement conflates texture with composition — a fundamental classification error. Correct evaluation requires applying the QAPF diagram: plot modal % of quartz, alkali feldspar, plagioclase, and ferromagnesian minerals.

questions.q: Design a field identification key (dichotomous, max 4 steps) that allows a Class 11 student to distinguish between granite, basalt, and gabbro using only a hand lens, HCl acid, and a geological hammer.
questions.a:
1. React with dilute HCl → fizz? YES → not these three (carbonate); NO → go to 2.
2. Crystal size visible to naked eye? YES → go to 3; NO (fine-grained/aphyric) → basalt.
3. Colour index (mafic mineral %): <30% (light) → granite; >60% (dark) → gabbro.
A poor key uses only colour ("pink = granite") ignoring that granites can be grey/white and gabbros can be greenish; it fails to use texture and mineralogy systematically.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Igneous rocks are rocks formed from the cooling and ______ of molten magma (below surface) or lava (on surface).

Fill in the blank: Start with a kitchen analogy: imagine cooling molten chocolate — slow cooling in a bowl makes large crystals (granite), rapid quenching on a cold plate makes a glassy solid (obsidian), and ______ cooling with stirring makes a porphyritic texture.
What is Igneous rocks? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Igneous rocks are rocks formed from the cooling and solidification of molten magma (below surface) or lava (on surface).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Igneous rocks?
questions.a: Students believe "granite = any light-coloured coarse rock" and "basalt = any dark fine rock." They miss that granodiorite, tonalite, and syenite are also light coarse rocks, and that dolerite (diabase) is a medium-grained mafic intrusive distinct from both basalt and gabbro.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can: (1) Identify granite, basalt, and gabbro from hand specimens or photographs using texture and mineral composition; (2) Explain how cooling history (depth, rate, water content) produces phaneritic, aphanitic, porphyritic, vesicular, and glassy textures; (3) Classify any given igneous rock into the IUGS QAPF scheme using modal.
